review_text_raw:
The best way to start the review is to mention that this is game is for everyone. It's designed to let even the least "techy" of the players understand the concept and how it works.

As someone who does quite a lot of work on command line on a daily basis, I can definitely say that the game is very friendly in that aspect, and that the developers did a lot of work on making it as realistic as possible, without having the players browse through endless 'man' pages of every command. And it has very positive effects. The simplification of the entire interface, of the commands themselves, makes for a nice introduction for people who never used it before, or for people who have some sort of irrational belief that the command line is only for "hacker gods". People who are already familiar with the command line interface on UNIX based systems will find some of the classic commands returning in this game.

It's not bad at portraying the way most of the black/gray-hat hacking is done. These days, the movies often portray hackers as some wizards who constantly type in various codes on the keyboard while looking at the 8 screen wall with various kinds of text/graphical output, analyzing them in mere seconds and breaking into NASA/CIA/FBI/KGB/<whatever else the movie's plot is about> servers. All that while looking cool. No, no and no. This is not how hacking generally looks like. Instead, as the game itself portrays, hackers merely use (or write) programs with specific purpose (such as PortHack) to do the work for them, while browsing through the Internet, listening to music &c.

Therefore, one could conclude that the game is pleasantly realistic. Yes, some things had to be cut short or ignored. Some tools could hardly work the way they work, or their principle was fixed many decades ago, but it's all excusable, seeing as the main point of the game is providing fun, not having the player spend countless of hours reading stuff on StackExchange and various documentation sites.

Graphics are not the amazing 4k ultra mega sharp masterpiece that in order to run you'd need the latest cutting edge graphics card. They are merely... good enough for the game. It relies heavily on the command line so there is not anything that you could do about it anyway. There are many different themes (packed in the x-server.sys) and each of them has a different background and music.

The music? That's entirely subjective. I did not try a lot of themes, but I could notice that in all of them, the sounds were primarily electronic. Some were pleasant and nice to hear, some were annoying. Personal preference, really. 

The game itself has many references to the real world. These references are based on various movies, games, stores &c. I personally find them as a small nice addition which may or may not give you that "AHA!" moment. Most of them are just hidden in various text files.

With that said, the story of the game is... decent. I do not wish to spoil any of its elements, but let's just say that it's not the most innovative one. It's not a game breaker. It servers well its function to drive the game forward, but don't expect some legendary cool story that will keep you on the edge wondering what will happen next. I did not play the game's add-ons and thus I can't talk about them. Perhaps they are better, or perhaps they are worse.

And now, comes the greatest problem I have found with the game itself. Exactly because the story is the way it is, the game feels too repetitive. It can get boring quite quickly, many times over. While playing the game, you generally have the same routine, hacking into another system (done on the same way almost every time), retrieving/deleting/reading a file, delete the logs, log out. Sure, there are tracers to make the process faster. The firewall analysis can be rather fun when combined with tracers, as you get to feel like some sort of a movie hacker trying to find the right combination while the time is running out. But everything else is, as said earlier, too repetetive and boring.

So when it all comes down to it: 

Gameplay: 6/10
Realism: 8/10
Story: 5/10
Bugs: 9/10 (not a single bug found, although that doesn't mean that one couldn't be there)
Graphics: 5/10 
Music: 6/10
Overall: 6.5/10

I would not recommend you to buy the game with its full price. It's just not worth it. But if you find it to be free, or on sale, and wish to indulge yourself into the world of command line and hacking, then go for it.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.


[h1] RATING: 8.5/10 [/h1]

review_text_raw:
[url=https://kinglink-reviews.com/2018/05/21/hacknet-review/] Full Review [/url] --  [url=http://store.steampowered.com/curator/31803828-Kinglink-Reviews/] Curator Site [/url]

Hacking games are weird. There are games with hacking as an ability such as Deus Ex or Watch Dogs but that’s not what I’m talking about. Those game have a “hacking mechanic” which at best is a mini-game and at worst is a button press. There are also games where the focus is on “hacking” systems and while it’s almost never realistic it usually can take steps in that direction and still be fun. Hacknet is one of those games, and it is an excellent example of why I enjoy those games.

So there are two sets of games I play. Normal games, stuff like Far Cry, Destiny, Bayonetta that average gamers can enjoy the same as me. Then there are the special games. I call them “programmer games” And they’re not all the same, they don’t have the same style of gameplay but most are made for the analytical mind of a programmer. Programmer games to me are games like Factorio, and pretty much every Zachtronics game (Which I will start reviewing soon, I promise, Zach your day will come!). And Uplink. Yes, Uplink is certainly there.

Uplink might be the first game I ever played where I felt a bond with the developer. I didn’t just like Uplink. I loved every minute of it. I was a novice with computers (and in some ways maybe I still am) but Uplink gave me the feeling that I was hacking into computers, and racing to beat a trace to avoid detection. Uplink was a blast. It was a great game. Hell in the back of my mind whenever I’m running a route trace (tracert) or pinging a server, I still imagine the map of the world and believe it’s following a single line on it.

I’m not the only person who liked Uplink. I can say that with absolute certainty because Hacknet clearly was developed to be similar to Uplink. Now two people can come up with the same idea, but Hacknet came out a decade after Uplink and even has a mission about someone copying “Introversion’s” game idea in Hacknet. Introversion is the name of the company that made Uplink.

Because of that, I’m sure the question comes up if this is a clone. While I have a very long version of why it doesn’t matter, the question would carry more weight if Hacknet didn’t differentiate itself from Uplink, or if Uplink was still developed. Introversion has gone on to make other amazing games, including the current “Prison Architect”. While Uplink is a clear inspiration, it’s also just the starting point, and Hacknet ran with it in so many directions that I’m impressed.

But there is one thought that Hacknet didn’t improve on Uplink. Uplink has a rather solid story, and it’s exciting from the first moment to the end of the game. I remember playing it a number of times, and the story drove me on to finish it in more than one way.

Hacknet, on the other hand, has a weaker story. Most of the story is done through missions and while there are some choices the player can make, or choose between a number of groups, there’s not really a reason or a purpose for it.

The real story of Hacknet only appears at the end and it only becomes a major event for a number of missions in a row, but it’s never has a strong pull to finish it, instead you just want to keep completing missions and because of that the story pulls you along. I feel like a lot of the story comes out of nowhere.

That’s not to say there are no interesting stories in Hacknet, but they’re more about the current mission you are on or just side stories that develop the world. It’s a shame because it’s one of the big flaws in the game in my opinion. The game feels like it tries to be open to the player making choices so it’s free-form but then backloads all the major story events to the end. I’d have loved to see the major story develop into emergency situations you deal with throughout the game and you could get the feeling you are competing against something even if you weren’t.

The bigger problem to me though is the story doesn’t tend to listen to the rules it has set up for its universe. You start the game and eventually join a hacking group. The first group are “White Hats” which means constructive hacking. They don’t exactly follow those rules, but while they can be destructive, they have a moral code that’s critical for them. It’s a good mantra to follow, and I like the idea of it.

The problem is the game never follows it up. In fact, a few missions are hollow when you realize there’s no positives or negatives for how you do jobs. The group might claim they’re “White Hats” and they told me to only delete what was necessary on one assignment. I trashed the computer and destroyed everything I could. The group never brought up my destructive nature. In fact, from that point onward, I found I could go against almost all the rules that the story developed for me.

For instance, Hacknet stresses deleting logs are important, and this was critical in Uplink. If you left logs in Uplink, people would be able to backtrace you even after you disconnected. However, in Hacknet there are two problems. First disconnecting from a server leaves a final log entry that’s deadly. In real life, you could wipe the log, have a program delete them after a timed execution or crash a server to avoid writing a disconnect if it matters. But none of these are required because of the second issue. Leaving the logs alone makes no difference. It’s a story element that doesn’t actually have gameplay attached to it.

I want to say both of these are acceptable and they are, but in fact, they annoy me a lot. The logs were a core system in Uplink and while the new game doesn’t have to be exactly like Uplink, Hacknet talks about deleting logs as critical. If they make it a major part of the story, they should require it since they said it was important.

So this has started to evolve into a discussion on the gameplay, and the gameplay is either the best part or the worst part of Hacknet. It will pretty much come down to the question of if the player can use a terminal effectively.

If you take a random server in Hacknet, you’ll usually be presented with a login prompt and the ability to “probe the network”. Almost always you will have to probe the network, from there the game will tell you what type of security measures the servers have. It might be a proxy server that you have to overload with other servers or a Firewall that means there’s an analysis program you have to run and figure out a passcode by reading off the letters that remain after analysis. You’ll almost always have to open ports on the system so you can crack the password, and you open ports by running exploits. Almost all of this is only done through the console. You can probe with the mouse, but the exploits require running the programs manually and giving them the ports.

The thing is, this is rather fun to me. I love the hacking aspects, and eventually when there’s a time limit it gets even better, trying to get everything done against a ticking clock because you have to run all the exploits, overload the proxy, figure out the firewall, and then do whatever you intended on the computer before it locks you out again.

The downside is the trace is always the same length of time. In Uplink there’s an idea of proxies which worked, as you could build a longer trace time but here, you just directly attack the computer and either have enough time, disconnect before you’re finished or run out of time.

There are games with hacking as an ability such as Deus Ex or Watch Dogs but that’s not what I’m talking about. Those game have a “hacking mechanic” which at best is a mini-game and at worst is a button press. There are also games where the focus is on “hacking” systems and while it’s almost never realistic it usually can take steps in that direction and still be fun. Hacknet is one of those games, and it is an excellent example of why I enjoy those games. So there are two sets of games I play. Normal games, stuff like Far Cry, Destiny, Bayonetta that average gamers can enjoy the same as me. Then there are the special games. I call them “programmer games” And they’re not all the same, they don’t have the same style of gameplay but most are made for the analytical mind of a programmer. Programmer games to me are games like Factorio, and pretty much every Zachtronics game (Which I will start reviewing soon, I promise, Zach your day will come!). And Uplink. Yes, Uplink is certainly there. Uplink might be the first game I ever played where I felt a bond with the developer. I didn’t just like Uplink. I loved every minute of it. I was a novice with computers (and in some ways maybe I still am) but Uplink gave me the feeling that I was hacking into computers, and racing to beat a trace to avoid detection. Uplink was a blast. It was a great game. Hell in the back of my mind whenever I’m running a route trace (tracert) or pinging a server, I still imagine the map of the world and believe it’s following a single line on it. I’m not the only person who liked Uplink. I can say that with absolute certainty because Hacknet clearly was developed to be similar to Uplink. Now two people can come up with the same idea, but Hacknet came out a decade after Uplink and even has a mission about someone copying “Introversion’s” game idea in Hacknet. Introversion is the name of the company that made Uplink. Because of that, I’m sure the question comes up if this is a clone. While I have a very long version of why it doesn’t matter, the question would carry more weight if Hacknet didn’t differentiate itself from Uplink, or if Uplink was still developed. Introversion has gone on to make other amazing games, including the current “Prison Architect”. While Uplink is a clear inspiration, it’s also just the starting point, and Hacknet ran with it in so many directions that I’m impressed. But there is one thought that Hacknet didn’t improve on Uplink. Uplink has a rather solid story, and it’s exciting from the first moment to the end of the game. I remember playing it a number of times, and the story drove me on to finish it in more than one way. Hacknet, on the other hand, has a weaker story. Most of the story is done through missions and while there are some choices the player can make, or choose between a number of groups, there’s not really a reason or a purpose for it. The real story of Hacknet only appears at the end and it only becomes a major event for a number of missions in a row, but it’s never has a strong pull to finish it, instead you just want to keep completing missions and because of that the story pulls you along. I feel like a lot of the story comes out of nowhere. That’s not to say there are no interesting stories in Hacknet, but they’re more about the current mission you are on or just side stories that develop the world. The first group are “White Hats” which means constructive hacking. They don’t exactly follow those rules, but while they can be destructive, they have a moral code that’s critical for them. An interesting mix between Uplink and Street Hacker, for the price of ~10 USD is definitely worth checking out.

The game is pretty fun, some things require attention to detail and logical thinking, and the humor is pretty good!

However, the game launched with a very bad bug which might make your save useless: if you try to make two missions at a time, you won't be able to complete the first one. This can simply kill your save.
Also, even though the presentation is well done and the interface looks pretty, I don't see much advance over what other Hacking games did before (Uplink was released in 2001), so you really should approach this with caution. The biggest difference here is being able to use both a GUI and a Console - which is good news.

This doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the game, of course. But it does dissapoint if you expected anything more than that.

I haven't finished the game yet, due to the bug that probably broke my savegame. But about the plot: it's decently intriguing and will make you want to uncover all the secrets, as a hacking game should.

So even though I ended up pretty disappointed - it's 2015, yet there's little news here. Even Street Hacker, which is a decade old and terribly programmed, had deeper features; and Uplink had a more compelling gameplay and story - there's still some fun to be had and some jokes/moments actually made me laugh or smile. 
I do recommend waiting for a patch before playing it, though. So rush it on your own risk.

review_text_raw:
To be fair Uplink is better. This game is good because you get to use the keyboard. Uplink is a hacking game where keyboard is not used, so the biggest flaw is now solved. Problem is the game lacks a bit of adrenaline. 

1) Most servers don't trace you, so you can just hang around forever.
2) Its not clear where you are connected too. Once you hack a place is there opened forever. You don't even have to disconnect.
3) You clear your logs but not the disconnected log, which makes no sense. In Uplink you have to clear logs at origin and destination, seems more realistic.
4) Its too easy to go up the ranking. 
5) In Uplink you had money to worry about. Upgrade hardware and buy software. In Hacknet all you get is reputation, that also have no impact besides gettings invitations.
6) The game does not allow you to accept more than 1 mission.
7) The storyline is a bit broken. I made 1 mission that lead to a hacker invading my computer, that leads to another mission and to another mission and basically you cannot accept other mission while the "story" is leading you in 1 way. That made me join an organization and now I cannot finish the old missions. Basically I lost 3 missions, cannot be played.
8) The game UI is a bit limited. I cannot open a file and an email at the same time. Which makes very annoying to take note to things. Althought I cannot complain much on that, as in Uplink I really had a pen and paper next to me all the time, in this game I never used real paper so far.
9) Uplink allow you to do other stuff, such as Stock Market, browse any server, etc. Hacknet is limited. You only get the servers IP when the game wants you to get. There is not freedom besides follow the story.
10) Uplink allows you to choose which mission to make, in the sense of choosing to be a good or a bad hacker. In Hacknet some missions presentation don't have more than 2 lines. You have to accept missions without even knowing what skills you need, what tools you need and what you have to do. Its really 1 path only. And if you try to get missions in different orders you lose them, just like I lost 3. UPDATE: Because of this 1 path only + cannot accept more than 1 mission, you can game over all the time. If you delete the wrong file, edit the wrong record, its finished. People call this bug in the forum, I call this lack of flexibility. In Uplink you could simply give up on a mission and pay a fine. If you delete a file you are suppose to upload, it shouldn't be game over, just some kind of punishment.
11) It uses Unix commands but limit them. For instance you have rm command but cannot be used to delete folders. Cannot download folders either.
12) Find it a bit weird that no special software is required to know when you are being traced.
13) So far the challenge of the game seems to be more about curiosity of the player. Meaning you have to look into every folder and file and read and see what you can find (be aware) rather than having a challenge on the hacking it self, such as limited time, required software, go throught LAN networks, etc.
14) You can hack a webserver, a main frame, a home pc or a cell phone, they all look the same, they all have same file structure, they are all hacked with same tools. A bit boring no?
15) Network map completely unecessary. Its just a harder way to find servers, if you are not going to use it to bounce like Uplink, why have that? Just a window with animated blue balls. A list with a search box and some favorites would do the job, or better, connect always using the line command, IP or name assigned by the user.
16) Once you scan a server and it reveals other computers connected to that, more "balls" appears and its a mystery why some are very distant and some are very close. The distance is based on what? It simple confuses the player as it adds a connection between them and with time the connections cross each other. Well, still trying to figure out why did it this way.
17) I'm already playing this game for hours and all I do is execute programs to open ports.


The good:

a) Very well done interface in the sense that keyboard and mouse usage is well integrated. The key here is keyboard. Its very nice to be able to play the entire game using keyboard only.
b) I like the fact that webserver have website with real images. Just because its a hacker game, it doesn't mean the "normal" internet doesn't exist. Although limited, I liked the www.cfc.com.
c) You can see an effort to bring interesting content to see around. Most servers have files that are not crucial to the missions, things you can read, chats, funny stuff. That really adds to the game and was one of the things I feel lacking in Uplink. Perhaps this is one of the reason a lot of servers don't have tracing mechanism, so you don't have time pressure all the time.
d) Not having time pressure all the time is good, but also removed money pressure and other stuff, which is left it a bit unbalanced.
e) Nice animations. The screens change a lot. Its not the same interface all the time.

review_text_raw:
I have never left a review here in on steam for anything....that in itself should make you appreciate just how strongly I feel about what I am about to say and just how absolutely and unequivocally true what I am about to say really is.

Let's start from the positives.....actually positive:
The graphics are OK....along with the music it does create an atmosphere appropriate to the setting of the game.
That's it.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU BUY:
1) The game is essentially a mishap collection of dubiously formatted XML files, along with the main executable of the game which is obviously just a parser along with the graphics engine (presumably). Although it is possible to play the game normally, I guarantee that you will soon waste your time trying to "fix" the myriad of issues that arise from the poor structure of the gameplay itself (more on that later) See my play time? 87 hours? Most of it has been spent scouring the internet on ways to fix broken missions, enable progression through other parts of the story, etc.
2)There are several limits to and aspects of the basic design that make NO sense. For example, yes, you can use a "terminal" with a few commands to progress through the game. These commands include options to open and close your actual CD tray (wow, how ARG of the author--when was the last time anybody used the CD tray for anything? when was the last time anybody saw a computer with an actual CD drive ???). HOWEVER IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO CREATE OR DELETE DIRECTORIES IN YOUR IN-GAME COMPUTER, NOR CREATE FILES..That's right....as crazy as it sounds, you can't even copy files on your own machine. The only way to create files is downloading them from somewhere else and then renaming them if you want to "fake" a simple copy command....but yes, if you want a game that opens your CD tray by all means, stop reading this now and buy the game. The terminal itself has no ability to scroll up, which sometimes means you need to retrace your steps if you forgot to jot some key piece of information down.
3)There is no hardware upgrade system, which means your hacking machine is what it is from beginning to end. It doesn't really matter for the most part, as the speed of the operations you perform in the game is largely dependent on your own ability and response time (that's the main game mechanic). However RAM is kind of important, because that's what all your hacking tools consume to run, as expected. The problem is that if you, for example have the notes app open with passwords and information about your current mission (thus avoiding the aforementioned backtracking in point 2) , you will run out of memory pretty quickly...forcing you to run programs one at a time and wishing you could actually make money in this game to buy more than 1 GB of ram (lol...seriously...just lol).
4)You can only accept 1 mission at a time (WHY...JUST WHY?!???!). This may not seem a big issue, but it is what literally breaks the game again and again. This ridiculous limitation means that you can't complete all the missions offered in the game because no matter what you do as you progress through the story the game forces you to move on and leave the unfinished missions behind, never to be played. review_text_raw:
I bought this game on sale, only paid a few bucks for it, and still feel a little ripped off. This possibly could be turned into a good game, but I doubt they'd make the effort. It feels kinda like it's not complete. I actually quit the game in frustration after they got what proxies do blatantly wrong. They paint proxies as some sort of more advanced firewall.
This could be a fun game. I actually like the idea of a terminal simulator hacking game. It seemed kinda cool. That's why I bought it. But it's not fun. The writing is poor, though there are a few humourous references to a few things, like Harry Potter for example. They didn't even bother to get a lot of common common technology right. Why are you using exe's in *nix environments? This is definitely Hollywood hacking. Worse yet, it's Hollywood script kiddie-ing. It feels like a game that could be thrown together very quickly by a small group of coders. Worse yet, they apparently have a very limited understanding of computers.
If they fix all the areas that are blatantly WRONG, and do a few bug fixes so the commands work more like terminal commands, and make the writing a bit more compelling, it might make for a good game. As it stands, I've played it once, and I don't know how soon I will again. It feels like a few bucks down the drain.
Oddly enough, I keep getting the urge to play a game like this, but then I remember how bad this was when I did play it.

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1]What is happening in the game:[/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
    [*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
    [*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
    [*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
    [*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
    [*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
    [*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
    [*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
    [*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
    [*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
    [*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
    [*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
    [*]This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.
[/list]

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

Greetings,
BirdCute

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

1. You can't finish all contracts. At some point the game will just tell you "You're good enough for more difficult tasks" and a main quest will trigger, blocking you from accepting new quests. You can never go back and you can't do them after the final mission.

2. You can't create files or directories. Organizing your downloaded files is annoying because you can only use the pre-defined ones. In one contract you're supposed to forge a file, and that works by downloading a file and editing the copy...

3. You can't remove directories. There's almost never a need to do so, but when you need to remove the contents from a directory with multiple subdirectories, you need to access each subdir individually and remove the contents.

4. Autocomplete doesn't add a whitespace after the autocompleteted word. Confusing as hell for a regular terminal user.

5. The final mission consists of multiple phases, which each one explaining your next goal. In phase 3 you're supposed to send a password but you aren't told so. I just used the password I found to login and continued my quest. After a while I got stuck, and after more than an hour I finally looked into a walkthrough - and learnt that I needed to send the password instead of entering it, and that had already solved the final mission by myself over an hour ago. At least I could just click the "complete quest" button 4 times in a row to trigger the ending.

6. The gameplay is quite repetetive. Connect to a server, open the closed ports (which always works the same, for all of them), find the file you need. There are only 2 missions that go beyond that and actually force you to think: The final mission, and the mission before. That doesn't really speak for the game.

7. The map is just plain awful. It's cluttered with nodes from earlier contracts which you never need to connect to anymore. Literally hardest part of the game is finding the correct node on the map.

8. Secrets. Don't get me wrong, secrets are great. But I looked into a guide after finishing the game, and some secrets didn't trigger for me although I definitely satisfied their conditions. So maybe I shouldn't have written "Secrets", but "Bugs". Furthermore, some secrets get you hyped, and when you finally solve their puzzle, you get... a digital clock that even uses up your RAM?

9. Alt+Tab closes the game.

I completed the game in a single session. It was kinda fun, although way too easy. But damn, some of the issues I just mentioned are pissing me off and I'm not going to play the DLC or any user-created mod.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What to expect if you're new to this game genre[/h1]
Hacknet is a new title in the otherwise stagnant, indie genre of hacking simulation games.
And a fresh breeze it is.

No doubt there is hardly any competition for this kind of quality.
Graphics are amazing, the hacking system introduced is quite good and consistent, it has gigantic potential for expansion that desperately needs to be used, and hopefully will. In it's current shape there might be little room for multiplayer gameplay, because of the game mechanics, but hopefully as the game gets finalized it will be implemented.

The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level.
Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying.
The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush.

Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember.

The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!)

[h1]Finally the 'Uplink vs Hacknet'[/h1]
Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink.
Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy.
The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging.
If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding.
Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet.

[h1]Final words[/h1]
Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date.
If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers.
Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1] What is happening in the game: [/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
[*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
[*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
[*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
[*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
[*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
[*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. [*]It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
[*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
[*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
[*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
[*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
[*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

This was Kedeajan,
Have fun!

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

This game is good. Just not great.

I actually didn't finish this game, but I read a story synopsis and it was, well, not too creative. Decent, but not amazing. The reason I didn't finish is because the story effectively takes a break for about 8-10 hours after the first hour, having you invest into smaller stories that you come across in small missions. The other reason I didn't finish was that the gameplay felt like actual hacking and work, and it was the kind of grindy, difficult work that one might receive in a classroom. Some features of the UI were extremely difficult to operate, and while that was somewhat realistic, I came to play a game, not because I liked doing difficult computer work, which is part of the reason why some hackers become hackers. Speaking of that, this game makes hacking extremely easy and simplified. I guess that if a hacking OS was developed in real life, it may actually be this easy, but in reality now hacking is way more difficult, complicated and sometimes more fun than this.

The world building and details were fantastic. I can't tell you how many times I laughed scrolling through logs on PCs I'd hacked into. They were well written and funny. But the massive break from the story made me feel like I was actually doing hacker work (although way too easy) and not playing a game. I came to experience a story, play a game, be something and someone else for a while, not to actually do hacker work. This game did not advertise as a hacker sim, but as a game where you play as a hacker with a story. That is my main problem with this game.

And don't get me wrong--I am all about games that require you do think and reflect and do not have big visuals or explosions or gunfights--this game's gameplay was boring. I've already said how the hacking was too easy and the UI was way too hard, but simply, hacking got boring rather quickly. That's basically it. In terms of additional information, there were no bugs and it was programmed very solidly. 

Overall, get this game when it is very cheap and play it for a few hours. You can have more fun with it than just two hours, so you don't have to return it, just buy it very cheap or free, that's how I got this game, it was free for a limited time and I downloaded it. 79/100 -- good, just not a B.

Final Update (3):
Seeing as the dev doesn't seem to give a damn anymore about providing the patches necessary to have the game work as advertised in a timely manner, I won't check on it or update the review any further.
Maybe the game will someday be what it should've been from day 1, but 3 weeks early access quality for a full release isn't acceptable.

-------------------------------------------------------------

Sadly, this has to be a [b]not recommended[/b] review.
The reason for this is the apparent lack of quality control before release. See details below.

First off, the concept is great. I really want to love this game for it's concept. It is basically a much better version of Uplink.
Now, is it realistic from a hacking point of view? No. But that's a good thing, because realistic hacking scenarios would be pretty boring for a game. The concepts are taken from the real world and simplified/modified to make an interesting game.

It is simple at first and doesn't get too difficult while still providing some challenges and a nice storyline. 

That being said, while the game could be a 9/10, game-breaking bugs currently make it at most a 4/10.

Here are some that I've encountered so far:
- You are able to take multiple contracts at some point, but doing so will prevent further progression due to the quest completion system being bugged.
- Using multiple profiles is inconsistent, you can't be sure that your savegame remains the way it was
- Game supports windowed mode but crashes regularly if you focus on another window
- Loss of all savegames - this is a big one. The last time the aforementioned crash occured, I've lost all of my saves.

The last bug on this list is the main reason this review has come to a not recommended conclusion and the others severely contributed.
If any beta testing would've been done, such a list of game-breaking bugs wouldn't exist.

Update 1: After the most recent patch promised a solution  to "many issues that were causing people to lose save files" I've decided to start a new profile. Did some work, saved session and exited the game normally. And alas, as I started the game again today there were no accounts and my save_accountsMeta.xml was gone. Again. This is clearly getting ridiculous and I wouldn't expect a solution any time soon, the dev will probably need a few weeks to figure out the issues with Steam API/Cloud saves etc.

Update 2: Since apparently fixing the savegame issues within a reasonable amount of time isn't happening, I have to say this is close to false advertising. The game should be tagged early access if the amount of issues is still that extensive after two patches. This is the sort of behaviour I'd expect from large companies that simply don't give a sh*t anymore, not form an indie dev trying to make his name. I hope the dev learns some things from this failed release, one of them being that you shouldn't release a game full of bugs when you're too busy being at conventions after the release and don't have time to fix the issues.

Don't get me wrong: everyone makes mistakes and stuff like that can happen. But that doesn't change the fact that as a customer I kinda feel cheated, since there's a reason I don't buy early access and this time the product isn't of higher quality.
Again, once the major bugs are fixed and solutions for the existing issues are presented, I'll gladly give this game a recommendation.

[h1]10/10 will play again & buy the DLC when I have money[/h1]

I got a free copy of [i]Hacknet[/i] from a promotion on Humble Bundle without really knowing what the game was and only started playing it because of the Spring Cleaning Event here on Steam. I only intended to play it for a little bit and then move on to something else.  ...I finished the game in one sitting. Which took most of the night when I was supposed to be sleeping and I barely even noticed. Never before would I have said that a game based almost entirely around typing computer run commands would hold my interest, but [i]man[/i] was I completely enthralled start to finish.

Not only did I finish the game in one sitting, but I also immediately started over to complete side quests and find bonus material I had missed the first time around. I still haven't finished the last achievement and found all the cool hidden bonus stuff.

[u]Plot[/u]
You have been introduced into the world of hacking by Bit, another hacker who has sent you a series of automated messages fearing his own demise. [spoiler]Yes, he is actually dead. I was about an inch away from crying when it was finally confirmed late in the game.[/spoiler] Through the course of the game you work with a number of hacker communities working both as a freelance digital vigilante and trying to unravel what really happened to Bit. The plot was exciting and I ended up emotionally invested. [spoiler]There is only one ending to the game, but there are optional side quests that alter way in which you get there, as well as bonus content that appears to only be available after a restart.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Most of the gameplay is done by typing various commands into your "terminal" in much the same fashion as old-school computer programs. If you've worked with DOS or similar systems you will probably have a bit of a leg up with the basic mechanics of the game. Using those commands you hack through the security systems of other computers, copying and deleting files off their harddrives and skipping from their computers to others in their network. These hacking attempts are sometimes straightforward, sometimes more complicated with critical thinking and puzzle cracking abilities required. The further you progress in the game the more difficult they become with most of the later hacking attempts becoming a fast-paced, speeding heart race against time. There is one(?) hidden mini-game that differs from this format. [spoiler]You can find it by taking the "Pointclicker" contract from Entropy[/spoiler] Overall, I didn't think the game was very difficult, although there were plenty of challenges to overcome. I did require a walkthrough the get myself out of a tricky spot, but that was mostly due to impatience. Probably the most difficult thing in the whole game was typing commands fast enough, so those who aren't good typists might struggle more with this game.

[u]Graphics & Music[/u]
[i]Hacknet[/i] has a very simple GUI for the entire game, fairly old-school computer but with a futuristic vibe. If the color scheme bothers you, just pay attention to the achievements. ;) [spoiler]My favorite was the L-e version, I do believe.[/spoiler] The music was all low-key techno music which I quite enjoyed. Sometimes it got a bit repetitive, but it changed according to where you were in the questline, so as long as you didn't get stuck in one place for a long time (like I did, before giving up and finding a walkthrough) it was fine.

[u]Bugs & Performance[/u]
Performance wise, the game ran perfectly well on my potato laptop with only 3GB of RAM. Since the game is done almost exclusively with the keyboard, having a real one is a must IMHO, but a mouse isn't necessary. I did just fine with a trackpad. The only "bug" I encountered when playing the game is that the game crashed whenever you tabbed out of it in fullscreen mode, even if you were chilling on the main menu. So make sure you save the game before attempting to open a different window!

review_text_raw:
While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).

After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):

[b]Pros:[/b]
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.

People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.

The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.

If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.

[i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i]

[b]Cons:[/b]

Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. 

[b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b]

Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.

To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).

Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

[b]OVERALL[/b]:
Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. 

For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.
