If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys. [i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i] [b]Cons:[/b] Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. [b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b] Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer. To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k). Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off. [b]OVERALL[/b]: Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

First things first, I loved the slick layout and visuals Hacknet plays quite nicely.  Music is pretty damn good too!

At first I really liked Hacknet as it feels like what Uplink should be in the modern gaming age.  You get cool looking interfaces, some psuedo-unix commands and maniplulations and a feeling of pressure as you hack your way past traces and logs.  However, thats where it falls apart a little.  You realise that logs are redundant and apart from an active trace when hacking some systems there are no repercussions to breaking log chains.  Except for one scripted event you dont need to worry about the men in black knocking on your door.  It was this attention to detail and consequnce that, in my opinion, gave Uplink its amazing gameplay.  I felt like the game needed that next level of complexity and difficulty to really come of age.

The major thumbs down however is game breaking bugs.  At time of writing this review there is at least one huge bug that is preventing the game being completed.  An attempt at fixing the bug was done but it did not solve the problem.  Cudos for the Developer at rushing to solve the issue but after one attempted patch there has been no communication on the status of the bug for about a month now.

Bottomline.  Its a fun little game but becomes one dimentional and easy once you realise there is no real way to lose apart from letting an active hack trace get you but even that is easily bypassed with one click or command.  The killer at this stage is bugs and more bugs.  I hope the game gets fixed and expanded, it could be a very nice game one day.


UPDATE:  The major bug has been fixed and I was able to finish the game.  Thanks to the Dev for fixing that up.
I have left my recommendation as negatvie which I am sad about as the game is pretty good.  The problem still is that its too easy once you realise there arent any repurcussions to not covering your tracks.  A little more depth would make this game a killer title!

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a game about hacking. The game opens with the Hacknet OS booting up with a message from a man named Bit, who says that if you see the message, he’s already dead. He leads you on a quest to start hacking, getting the attention of one hacker group, then a second, all to avenge his death and prevent the distribution of a hacking program.

The story itself is kind of mediocre, but it is serviceable; at its core, it is a story of corporate greed, as well as a revenge story, though by the end of it, it is pretty clear that the whole thing isn’t really as sinister as it appeared at first.

The real core of the story is the hacking – you log into various computers, break through their security mechanisms, and then are lead onto other computers. Spicing things up are timers, various mechanisms you have to bypass, and the various files and passwords and IPs you have to find to lead you on the next leg of your hunt.

Sadly, the game is plagued with poor design decisions. There are various points at which it isn’t clear what you’re supposed to be doing, and you’re left confused, only to find out you needed to hit the “reply” button on an email after breaking into a server to move on – despite the fact that the email wasn’t clear about that. At other times, you have to send them messages, and while this is usually clear (sending them an IP or password), on occasion it is not and ends up being rather frustrating.

Worse (and even more frustrating) are some outright bugs – situations where the game simply does not function like it is supposed to. Beyond there being some lost forevers in the game which are less than obvious, there’s additionally the fact that sometimes the game simply bugs out and won’t let you progress or do various things. You get a “mission incomplete” message when trying to proceed, and there’s simply no clear way around the issue. Indeed, two of the achievements require you to do things which simply don’t function half the time or more, judging by the many frustrated players who had to restart the game time and again to try and get them to work.

The UI itself is a bit obtuse at times as well; several of the hacking programs you use require additional bits of typing to execute, despite the fact that in many cases it literally never matters – it is always exactly the same number you have to punch in. And while it is neat seeing it use actual hackerish commands, ultimately there’s a lot of little pieces which just feel annoying to have to do time and again.

The only real good thing about the game is its aesthetics; which do work pretty well for what it is.

In the end, you aren’t really rewarded for your frustration. The core idea is cute enough, but in the end the game ends up being rather repetitive, and there just isn’t enough variation in the core gameplay. A mediocre story combined with sometimes unclear gating mechanics to make the game advance is just not a winning recipe for a game.

The game seems like a neat idea at first, but it just ends up being more frustrating than enjoyable to play. It isn’t worth your time or your money.

[i]Note: I am biased because of the nature of my job. While not related to IT Security, it involves technical troubleshooting / problem solving and all kind of investigations. Basically, less fun version of Hacknet.[/i]

[h3]Accurate Hacking Simulator?[/h3]

I was not exposed to a lot of hacking in games, maybe just a bit in Sleeping Dogs, or Cyberpunk 2077. While other games focus purely on hacking vibes, those tend to ignore the actual process. And Hacknet pays much more attention to the realistic aspect of the game.

Of course, to me it looks like huge oversimplification, but that was made as a game, right? It was made to be simple, fun and accessible. And it never felt like I am working, it felt like I am playing a game and having a good time. So while not being accurate, it nails the realistic hacking experience to enough extent. 

[h3]Handholding or Exploration?[/h3]

The first 60% to 70% percent of the game felt like a tutorial. Fun, with a lot of stories and action, but with a huge sense that I am playing in a sandbox. Everything is pretty safe, and you get what you need to do right from the email, so you need to execute specific steps without much investigation. Yes, you need to look for something specific, but it is usually very algorithmic and follows the same steps. 

So, this feels like handholding to me, and having to "detective" part to it, where you just don't know where to look at and have to think and explore. 

But! There are endgame quests, such as the main story line or Project Junebug quest. Those actually did things perfectly as I have wanted. There is more to reading, investigating, searching and connecting pieces of information together. This was perfect. 

Example: usually it would be "find a (file / password / IP) or edit / remove something. Here is the server.". That is straightforward. 

Project Junebug: Here is the name of the person. Kill him. 

You see what I mean? That is perfect example of what I wanted this game to be. And it eventually has things that appeal to me! So, overall, great experience. Right?

[h3]A bit of so-so moments[/h3]

Just one. The game has netMap, a graph that displays the machines you have connected to. And the graph grows, and there is less and less space, it all  becomes cluttered at some point. And there is no way to clean it up, resize, organize or alter. And this is sad a bit, because the missions that I liked involve a lot of research, but the research progress was hevily impacted by overall messy navigation system. 

But it's a minor thing. What else?


[h3]The Easter Eggs and Secrets[/h3]

While the big part of the game feels like a tutorial, it has a lot of things to explore. Jokes and memes, hidden quests with high rewards - it's all there. So if you want, you can take much more from the game than it offers at a first sight.

Like in some RPGs you can even get overpowered pretty early - if you follow some clues in the game, you can get CLOCK.EXE, which makes game itself hacked. Things that are hidden and require exploration definitely cool here.

[h3]The Music[/h3]

I pay a lot of attention to game OSTs, it makes me love the game more if the music resonates with me. And back in 2017 when I have bought the game, I learned about Hacknet from Remi (The Algorithm) - one of the musicians behind the OST, and I bought it. So, to me the OST is perfectly fitting the game. Just very neat, I thought. Until the final mission.

I have three examples of getting goosebumps from the music in the game:
1. One optional boss fight in Baldur's Gate 3
2. Expedition 33 in various places.

And... Yeah, the final mission of Hacknet! Putting [spoiler]Carpenter Brut's Roller Mobster[/spoiler], one of my favorite synthwave / darksynth tracks ever made me freeze for a minute in awe. And then realize that time is ticking and I need to do everything fast. Perfect sense of adrenaline. Great choice for OST!

[h3]Really solid hacking-lite experience[/h3]

Overall, I liked this game. Relatively short, but never gets dull. And I have not even touched the DLC yet - and it has 97% positive rating! So, while the main game is over for me, I will get to Labyrinths in future to feel this enjoyment again.

I have been waiting for the game to start, and now that I'm halfway through I've given up. It's boring and pointless. There is no story, there are no choices (even though the game wants you to think there are). That aside, it's not really a hacking game. "Hacking" just means typing the same commands and waiting for them to execute... every time... for every PC in the network.

Another big problem is that the game implies that it will use real world logic but then it doesn't. Like I can't execute a file on a PC I'm connected to? Since when? 

Instructions are never clear and even if they are I hate that the game forces me to only do things how the dev intended. Specifically for advcancing missions, it's never clear whether I just need to read the file or send it or send the password contained in it. All of those should work, not just one!

There are bugs - mostly soft locks, which is unacceptable for such a simple game.

Instead of spending time on the visualizations for each tool the dev should have spent time designing mechanics around them. For instance the firewall analyzer is okay. Not fun, but it's not completely idle, you have to do something. Each tool has to be like that, there has to be some mini-game associated with it, or there has to be some strategy as to which tools are used in what order.

I don't know what the music was like. It was so repeptitve so annoying I turned it off and played Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines OST. 

The only thing I liked about the game is the environmental storytelling. The chat logs sound EXACTLY like the Old Internet days. Kudos to the author for the research!

I'm not entirely sure what the target demographic is for this game. It's an ostensibly terminal-based game running on a UNIX platform, but it has minimal overlap with bash commands, and trying to treat it like bash will only get you confused. 

So, this must be aimed at people without any tech background. However, how much fun can someone uninterested enough in coding to not care about this have, if all they're doing is typing in the same auto-completing commands over and over into a terminal?

Oh, and you can't scroll on the terminal, too. On the other hand, the GUI is both cluttered and unintuitive. Everything feels horrid to use.

It claims to feature "REAL HACKING", but the hacking consists of running magic hack spells via the terminal, and, if you DO know anything about hacking, that makes a lot of what the game asks of you feel obtuse. It took me so long to realise that I was supposed to open up a shell on my own PC, which, if crashed, would somehow take down a proxy server hosted elsewhere? I was assuming I had to find some kind of initial access mechanism to bypass the proxy and execute shellcode on the target PC, but, uh, I guess crashing the equivalent of cmd.exe on my computer really is the future of hacking.

The story is okay, I guess. At least it was easy to 100%.

My advice to anyone interested in a hacking-type game aimed at beginners is to check out the (free!) OverTheWire Bandit wargame, instead; it's fun, and it'll actually teach you something useful.

review_text_raw:
There are clear influences from Uplink, but Hacknet stands on its own two feet for many design decisions.

Hacknet requires a lot of typing due to the text console. This brings a level of realism which is enjoyable, and the countdown timers do not seem to require the player to type at 200 words per minute. However, a few actions can also be initiated by mouse using a graphical user interface. The use of the mouse is a bit incoherent: those features which can use the mouse and those which cannot feel arbitrary and without obvious design merit.

There are a number of little bugs here and there. Head over to the discussions and check the bug report thread. Many of the valid bugs reported actually have more to do with polish. It's unfair to call them bugs, but fixing the issues could enhance the game's polish and lead to better immersion. There are a few actual bugs that can lead to gameplay issues, but they seem to be few and far between.

The story is a bit linear. I have found it hard to explore the networked universe outside where the missions take me. Compare this to Uplink, where there are a great many ways to find and access computers by goofing around. Computers tend to have random snippets from bash.org , which are humorous logs of conversations that reportedly happened on IRC. It's a nice touch as a reward for looking at systems and it makes them feel a little more fleshed out, yet the contents tend to be disconnected from any of the game's context. The snippets simultaneously help and hurt immersion.

Creative expression is available in small doses, but I do not consider this any kind of sandbox game. The potential for such a thing is there. For example, there are computers which run web servers. You can modify the HTML, and when you visit the web server, your changes are visible. It can be amusing to deface a virtual server even if no other living being will see it. However, if you delete all the system files from a computer and then forcibly shut it down, it should prevent the system from rebooting. This would destroy a system. In Hacknet, if you do this, the system will disappear from your network map for a little while and then come back (while still lacking system files). As a related polish-bug: you can immediately connect to any computer "destroyed" this way using the command console, even if the network map does not show the system as online.

The music is electronica-themed to suit the stereotype of a computer hacker. The sound track brings good ambience. I personally start to notice the repetitious nature of the music after playing 2-3 solid hours, but that's usually a good time to take a break anyway.

The recent release for Linux/Mac is welcome, except that has introduced a number of new bugs that need to be squashed. Save game interoperability is a current problem that needs to be resolved at the time of this writing. Linux/Mac support has its own thread in the game's Steam discussion area. I'm sure those problems will be resolved soon enough, but they are worth reading through before purchasing if you plan to play on Mac or Linux.

Overall, I'd say Hacknet is a fun puzzle game with a solid computer hacker theme. It could use more polish and the design decisions regarding keyboard or mouse interfacing could use some rethinking. As a professional programmer and IT person, I cannot really say with certainty if this game is accessible to non-programmers or non-IT people. I suspect the game is approachable enough to anyone who has ever had to type commands into anything instead of clicking glittery UI buttons.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is pretty much what it says on the tin - a hacking-themed game in which you must meet escalating challenges throughout the course of its story, which opens with a posthumous message coming from a hacker who has disappeared.  Stop right there, though - the story isn't very strong on the conspiracy and ends up being a missed opportunity, so don't dive in just yet.

Those not familiar with command-lines need not fret as this isn't a full-blown OS simulator like other games in the genre.  While it does have its own level of CLI sophistication, the tutorial and pacing thereafter is carefully crafted as not to overwhelm the inexperienced.  Anyone looking to roleplay a super hacking machine can comfortably play this game without having a manual in front of them (though a notepad may help).  Rather than have you coding a bunch of exploits or what have you, your hacking terminal - which is beautifully-rendered, btw - is loaded with magical tools that do all the work for you.  You just need to handle the set up, if you will, and the software will do the rest.

What separates Hacknet from others in the genre is its combo of command-line terminal and graphical user interface (think X-Window).  The game is aesthetically pleasing to the eye with a mix of hi- and low-tech, giving the interface an authentic OS feel.  If you're not keen on typing every little thing (which you can absolutely elect to do), you can instead click on the GUI to navigate around most of the systems and poke around.  You'll still need to key in some commands, but there's a good balance here if you want to save some time with navigation and reading files.  Websites aren't functional, but they do appear in the game and give it that extra little flavor, with one exception being a Clicker game that you can waste time on should you so choose to.

So while the story doesn't really play out in the best of ways, the hacking is quite fun... at least for the first little bit.  It very soon becomes repetitive because ultimately the puzzles are limited.  You will be taking on contracts/jobs from message servers and they each boil down to a) get into the target system and b) grab some information or delete stuff.  Even though you are introduced to new tools (and thus, the difficulty of breaking into a system increases), the game rarely deviates from this formula, even when the story demands it.  It's not really until the latter quarter of the game when you're doing interesting stuff, not so much because the repetitiveness is gone, but more because the answers aren't quite as obvious.

I would have liked to have a more involved tale form throughout the game and as I said above, it's a missed opportunity.  It would make discovery so much more satisfying.  This isn't made much better by most servers being devoid of anything interesting other than some randomly-pulled bash quotes which, if you've been around on the Internet long enough, you've already read.  Still, this is a minor nitpick and beyond that, there was nary an issue with the game.  I encountered no bugs or crashes, except that I wasted a good 2 or 3 hours trying to go down a different path (which happens under very, very specific circumstances), which highlighted the inability to save-where-you-want; basically, failing to meet the conditions, even though I thought I knew what I had to do, meant that I had to restart from scratch repeatedly just to get there... however, this alternate path is completely optional and easily-missed.  I only put this here as a warning to achievement hunters.

At the end of the day, Hacknet is a fun game that captures the spirit of hacking without overwhelming the player.  I'm sure there are more hardcore games in the genre, but at that point - in my opinion - I feel it stops being a game and starts being a job.  Hacknet manages to find the right balance between authenticity and Hollywood fantasy so it's a very enjoyable experience.

Just be aware that the blue screens look incredibly authentic.  Don't panic.

review_text_raw:
This game is... mediocre. The gameplay is monotonous and unchallenging, the storyline is fractured and uninspiring (it's even harder to take seriously since you're playing as a script kiddie), and the material is extremely far from reality.  As an actual Linux sysadmin, I am in particular annoyed by how poorly implemented common UNIX utilities are.  "ls *" and "rm ./*" fail, but "rm *" works? No "cp" or "mkdir"?  No way to delete directories? I can go on and on. Literally, I programmed more coreutils in a single college project than there are in this game. Couldn't they have just used busybox or something?  It certainly would have solved the issues the game has with file duplication in directories, since it'd be using actual files, rather than what is presumably a stack/queue/list/whatever.  And I would kill for io redirection.
Also, I'm mildly triggered by the executables being .exe files, but I'm definitely amused that you BSOD instead of kernel panicking.
I bought this game for a song, but I don't think I'd even recommend it if it were free, because in the time it takes you to play this game, you could have learned all sorts of actual UNIX commands in an actual terminal emulator on Linux, something that actually is free -- and you'd probably have a lot more fun, too.

BUGS:
- You can wipe the logs on any server without admin access.
- 89.220.121.48:/eos/apps/birds_8 is listed twice.
- Leaving a server and coming back resets the trace timeout without resetting your progress, which means that the trace timeout never actually matters.
- Uploading a file to a path containing another file with the same name, results in two files with the same name.
- The password for the Timekeeper's Vault doesn't actually work.
